{"slots": {"question": [{"claim": "Whether the Democratic 'convicted criminal' label on Trump spilled over to Democrats' perceptions of people with criminal records and of representation, and whether a counter-narrative could offset any such spillover.", "quotes": [{"text": "propagating such labels on Trump may thereby spillover, impacting constituents’ perspectives of individuals with records more broadly", "page": 1}]}],
"central_claim": [{"claim": "Exposure to the Trump ad labeling him a 'convicted criminal' lowered Democrats' perceptions of people with records, and a formerly system-involved representative's perspective shown before the ad largely offset that effect.", "quotes": [{"text": "Findings suggest that the counter-stereotype vastly ameliorated the negative effects of the advertisement on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with criminal records.", "page": 1}]}],
"evidence": [{"claim": "The evidence is a survey experiment with 2,439 self-identified Democrats in the U.S., assigned roughly evenly to a control group, a Trump ad alone group, and a counter-narrative first group. The ad was a Trump mugshot labeled 'CONVICTED CRIMINAL'. The survey was fielded through Prolific.", "quotes": [{"text": "the 2,439 participants were allocated approximately evenly across one of three different treatment groups", "page": 4}, {"text": "President Donald J. Trump’s mugshot, which was labeled, in all capital letters, “CONVICTED CRIMINAL.”", "page": 5}, {"text": "The survey was fielded through Prolific, an online survey platform that is commonly utilized for conducting survey-based research", "page": 8}]}],
"key_findings": [{"claim": "Exposure to the Trump ad alone significantly lowered Democrats' positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records relative to no ad exposure.", "quotes": [{"text": "exposure to the Trump advertisement alone significantly decreased positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records", "page": 11}]}, {"claim": "Placing a system-impacted state representative's perspective before the ad almost entirely offset the ad's negative effect on perceptions of people with records.", "quotes": [{"text": "when paired with (and preceded by) a counter-narrative of a dedicated, system-impacted state representative who speaks to the harm of the “criminal” label, these effects were almost entirely ameliorated", "page": 15}]}, {"claim": "The counter-narrative significantly reduced support for the Trump ad compared with the ad alone.", "quotes": [{"text": "exposure to the counter-narrative significantly decreased support for the Trump advertisement, relative to the Trump advertisement alone", "page": 11}]}, {"claim": "Exposure to the Trump ad alone significantly increased respondents' feelings of being well represented and their belief that officials serve the public, a result the authors did not hypothesize for representation quality.", "quotes": [{"text": "Additionally, exposure to the Trump advertisement significantly increased feelings of being well represented by elected officials", "page": 15}]}, {"claim": "The effects of the ad and counter-narrative on perceptions of people with records were larger for system-impacted respondents than for others.", "quotes": [{"text": "In terms of relative magnitude, the effects were greater for those who identified as being system-impacted, compared to those who did not", "page": 14}]}],
"scope_and_limits": [{"claim": "The design was not a full factorial, so the counter-narrative's effect alone cannot be isolated from the Trump ad, since the counter-narrative arm always includes the ad.", "quotes": [{"text": "the counter-narrative arm cannot be directly compared to the pure control arm to test the impact of the counter-narrative alone because it also involves exposure to the Trump advertisement.", "page": 16}]}, {"claim": "The study was conducted in July 2025, after the election, so the results may not hold during a campaign.", "quotes": [{"text": "this current study was conducted in July of 2025, after the outcome of the election was known and not actively during the campaign", "page": 17}]}, {"claim": "The authors describe the study as preliminary and say well-powered field experiments are needed to confirm and extend the findings.", "quotes": [{"text": "While well-powered and aptly-timed field experiments are needed to confirm and extend these findings", "page": 1}]}],
"theoretical_positioning": [{"claim": "The authors place the study within social categorization theory and extend it to argue that a stigmatizing label applied to one salient group member spills over to the wider category of people with records.", "quotes": [{"text": "social categorization theory [12–15] would suggest that the effects of utilizing this label likely spilled over.", "page": 2}]}, {"claim": "The authors offer Prospect Theory as a possible account of the finding that the Trump ad raised ratings of other officials, treating Trump as a reference point.", "quotes": [{"text": "Collectively, these results may simply be Prospect Theory in action: Donald J. Trump may be serving as reference point that may influence Democrats to see other elected officials as comparatively better", "page": 15}]}],
"interlocutor_claim": [{"claim": "Prior literature shows that labels such as 'criminal' cause worse perceptions of people with records than person-first language. The authors take this as the basis for expecting the Trump label to harm perceptions of people with records.", "quotes": [{"text": "Extant literature highlights the causal impact of propagation of labels, such as ‘criminal’, to significantly worsen perceptions of individuals with records, relative to more humanizing, person-first language", "page": 2}]}]}}
